newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: No early cut in SAfrica interest rates - Old Mutual.
newsitem.headline: No early cut in SAfrica interest rates - Old Mutual.

text.p: South African interest rates would remain high for some time as the country's meagre foreign exchange reserves ruled out an early cut, Old Mutual chief economist Dave Mohr said on Tuesday.
But an easing could be seen in the second half of 1997 if economic fundamentals improved.
Mohr said that economic growth would fall to 2.5 percent this year down from just over an estimated three percent in 1996, but predicted that the slowdown would be shortlived.

He said the level of the reserves was "dangerously low", covering not even five weeks' of imports. This could be exacerbated by another tumble in the rand, which would speed up capital outflows, or a deterioration in the current account.
"Even if the improvement in the current account continues, lower import tariffs and continued weak commodity prices could limit the extent of the recovery," Mohr said in a statement.

South Africa's trade surplus leapt to 2.04 billion rand in December on a sharp slowdown in imports and compared with a 378 million rand surplus in November. Economists have predicted imports slowing further and exports picking up in 1997.

However, Mohr said that domestic demand was still surprisingly strong and there was little evidence that the spending side of the economy was cooling. Government spending also remained strong, rising by almost 15 percent in the first nine months of the fiscal year.
One option for South Africa was to use foreign loans to shore up the reserves, but this would at best yield very limited results, he said.

He cautioned that a cut in interest rates could only be considered once the rand showed distinct signs of sustained stability and money supply growth, where M3 growth has clung to around 15 percent, would have to slow significantly.

"If domestic spending cools as expected, foreign exchange reserves improve markedly, inflation turns around and fiscal discipline is maintained, interest rates could be cut during the second six months," Mohr said.

He was also optimistic about economic growth in the longer term, despite a slight cooling off this year, as the combination of political transition, international re-integration and economic deregulation raised the economy's growth potential.
A speedy implementation of government's macroeconomic plan, a five-year economic plan unveiled in June last year, may go a long way in unlocking this potential, he said.

Although total demand was seen halving from an estimated four percent his year, producers would see some early relief after a tough 1996 as a more competitive exchange rate eased pressures on profit margins.
Consumers were in line for a tight year as taxes and inflation cut into spending which was seen slashed to 1.5 percent compared with four percent in 1996.
"With a large load of debt to service at painfully high interest rates, credit based spending growth should slow considerably," Mohr said.
